title: A mother's empty heart
hook: Musa's mother's heart became empty, and Allah steadied it (28:10)

segments.voice: Yesterday, the question in An-Naml, and your line was he answers the distressed. Who did you check in on, and how were they? Day five hundred twenty-four, and a new surah.

Surah Al-Qasas, the Stories, the twenty-eighth, tells Musa's life from the very beginning. And it begins not with Musa but with his mother. Pharaoh is killing the newborn boys of the Children of Israel. She has just had a son. And she is told, by an inspiration from God, to nurse him, and when she fears for him, to put him in a basket on the river. Don't fear, don't grieve, the verse says: We will bring him back to you. So she does it. She sets her baby on moving water and lets go. Then comes the next morning.

The Qur'an doesn't skip over what she felt. Pickthall: "And the heart of the mother of Moses became void". Empty. The Arabic is farigh, emptied out, vacant. Commentators asked: empty of what? Many said empty of everything except Musa. She couldn't think of anything else. Others said empty of patience, or of the calm she'd had the night before. Anyone who has waited outside an operating room knows the feeling. The verse goes on: she was about to give him away, to blurt out that the child was hers, had God not strengthened her heart. The word there is rabatna, We tied, We bound. It's the image of tying something so it doesn't drift: a horse, a boat, a heart. And the verse says why: so that she would be among the believers, those who trust. Notice what God doesn't do. He doesn't take the fear away. Her heart is still empty. He ties it down so that it holds. Then she does something very practical. She tells Musa's sister, follow him. The girl watches from a distance as the basket reaches Pharaoh's household. The baby refuses every wet nurse. And the sister steps forward and says, shall I show you a family who will look after him? So Musa comes home, fed at his own mother's breast, paid for by Pharaoh. The verse says it was so that her eye would be cooled and she wouldn't grieve, and so she would know God's promise is true. The empty heart is in the story on purpose. Faith here isn't the absence of panic. It's a heart held steady while it's still afraid.
screen: `HER HEART BECAME EMPTY.` · `RABATNA: WE TIED IT DOWN.` · `THE SISTER FOLLOWS THE BASKET.` · `HOME TO HIS MOTHER.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: steady someone who is afraid. Sit, and let the breath settle. Think of someone you know who is waiting for something frightening right now. Results, a court date, a child far from home, a hospital bed. Picture their face. Notice what they might need: not advice, not cheerfulness, just someone to sit with them so their heart doesn't drift. Decide what you can offer this week, a call, a visit, a meal, a message that says I'm here. If you pray, you can ask that their heart be tied steady. The bell holds the time.
A mother's empty heart. Musa's mother after the river, her heart emptied of everything but her son, and held steady by God until he came home. Today's word.
Your line: a heart held steady. Today, send the message to the person you thought of. Keep it short, and don't try to fix anything. Day five hundred twenty-four.

howItsDone: Muslims read the story of Musa's mother in Al-Qasas as a picture of trust in God under fear, and many recite its promise, We will bring him back to you, in times of separation.

it says her heart became empty, and she nearly gave him away.
God strengthened her heart rather than removing the fear
rabatna: He tied it down so it would hold.
Musa was nursed by his own mother in Pharaoh's household
his sister pointed Pharaoh's people to her, and he came home.

fork.setup: you're Musa's mother. the basket has gone downriver. your heart is empty, and you could run and shout that he's yours. what do you do?
options: run to the palace and claim him.
tell his sister to follow him.
fork.reveal: held steady by God, she sends his sister to follow the basket, and through her, Musa comes home.

original.note: Arabic: empty, vacant; the word for the heart of Musa's mother in 28:10.

trapdoor: what you thought: a brave mother who trusted God.
what it means: a mother whose heart was emptied by fear, and held steady by God so that she didn't fall apart.
what a scholar hears: fu'aduha farigha, 'her heart became empty', then rabatna 'ala qalbiha, We bound her heart, and 28:13's cooling of the eye: the Qur'an keeps her fear in the story.

sources.quoted: And the heart of the mother of Moses became void

sources.ref: Qur'an 28:7–13 (the river, the sister, the return)

notes: Pickthall 28:10 opening quoted from memory ('became void'); confirm.
Commentators' readings of farigh (empty of all but Musa; empty of patience; some read empty of grief) summarized; confirm.
The Arabic in 28:10 uses fu'ad (heart) for 'empty' and qalb in 'rabatna 'ala qalbiha'; trapdoor reflects this. Confirm.
'Paid for by Pharaoh' is a commentators' detail (the wet-nurse was paid); the verse says only that he was restored to her. Confirm or soften.
